passage: The school bus horn sounded at the corner, and Rehana still had one shoe on. 'Worksheet?' Ammi called. Rehana froze. She had spent last evening building a water-cycle model from a plastic bottle and cotton wool, so absorbed she had forgotten dinner, and the signed worksheet was somewhere. So was her water bottle. 'Every day, Rehana! Every single day!' Ammi's voice rose. Rehana's eyes stung. She wasn't trying to forget. Her older sister Zainab dug the worksheet out from under the model, squashed but whole, and pushed it into the bag. That evening Zainab taped a card to the door with five drawings: bottle, tiffin, worksheet, pencil box, shoes. 'Touch each one before you go,' she said. 'Like a game.'

qa.q: What did Rehana build the evening before?
qa.a: A water-cycle model from a plastic bottle and cotton wool.

qa.q: How did Rehana feel when Ammi shouted 'Every day'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and ashamed, her eyes stinging, because she wasn't forgetting on purpose.

qa.q: Why might Zainab's card work better than scolding?
qa.a: It turns remembering into a simple picture routine Rehana can touch each morning, instead of leaving her feeling bad.

qa.q: What is the rushed morning like for Ammi?
qa.a: Ammi is stressed and frustrated, with the bus waiting and the same things missing again, which is why her voice rose.

grounding: Shows a child who loses worksheets and bottles while absorbed in bursts of interest, feels bad when scolded, and is helped by a visual checklist.

passage: Lavanya had ignored the science project for three weeks. Then on Thursday night, after reading about bees, she built a cardboard hive with forty hexagons and stayed up till eleven. On Friday, Rafiq Sir held it up for the class. Then he asked for the maths worksheet. Lavanya went through her bag twice: a bee drawing, an old bus pass, a hair clip. No worksheet. Her face burned. 'Sorry, Sir. Again.' Two boys snickered. At break Rafiq Sir called her over and handed her a clear yellow folder with two labels: HOMEWORK IN, HOMEWORK OUT. 'Everything goes here, nowhere else. Show me on Monday.' Lavanya held it with both hands, the colour of her hive.

qa.q: What did Lavanya build on Thursday night?
qa.a: A cardboard hive with forty hexagons.

qa.q: What does Lavanya's face burning suggest?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and ashamed at forgetting the worksheet again, especially with two boys snickering.

qa.q: What made Rafiq Sir's folder a better response than a scolding?
qa.a: It gave her one clear place for homework and a small check on Monday, a routine that helps rather than shames.

qa.q: How might Rafiq Sir see Lavanya after the hive?
qa.a: He likely sees a capable, eager child who works in bursts, not a lazy one, which is why he offered help instead of punishment.

grounding: Shows a child who works in bursts of interest and keeps losing worksheets, and a teacher who offers a simple routine instead of a scolding.

passage:
'Ira Didi, don't tell Papa.'
'Tell him what?'
'The bottle. The blue one. It's gone.'
'That's the third one this term, Hemant.'
'I know!' His voice cracked. 'I put it down to catch a grasshopper at recess, then the bell went. I'm not lazy. I don't do it on purpose.'
'I know you're not lazy. You drew that whole grasshopper in ten minutes. Your brain just runs after the interesting thing.'
'So what do I do?'
Ira held up a metal clip from her drawer. 'This goes on the bottle. The bottle clips to your bag. It never comes off, even for grasshoppers.'
'Even really big ones?'
'Especially those.'
Hemant almost smiled. 'Will you tell Papa?'
'We'll tell him together. And show him the clip.'

qa.q: Why did Hemant put the bottle down at recess?
qa.a: To catch a grasshopper.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when his voice cracked?
qa.a: He felt upset and ashamed, worried about being called lazy when he never forgets on purpose.

qa.q: What did Ira get right in helping Hemant?
qa.a: She believed he wasn't lazy and gave him a simple fix, a clip that keeps the bottle on his bag, instead of a lecture.

qa.q: Why might Ira say 'We'll tell him together'?
qa.a: Ira seems to guess Hemant is scared of Papa's reaction, and wants to stand beside him while showing the plan.

grounding: Shows a child who keeps losing bottles when interest pulls him away, feels bad about it, and is helped by a simple routine rather than scolding.

passage:
Saturday, 11.40 p.m.
The timetable said: Chemistry 4 to 7, Maths 8 to 10. Instead: Lokesh's cousin's wedding. Mummy said I had to come, so I sat at the reception with my green highlighter in my pocket like an idiot. Lokesh kept saying, 'Relax, it's one evening.' But I could feel the chemistry slots going red in my head. Came home and crossed out today's box so hard the pen went through. Then I wrote: Sunday, 6 a.m. to 11 p.m., no breaks, no cricket for a week. Now I'm looking at it and it looks like a punishment, not a plan. Is that what it's turned into? The colour-coding used to make me feel calm. Tonight it just makes me feel guilty.
Francis

qa.q: What did Francis's timetable plan for Saturday?
qa.a: Chemistry 4 to 7 and Maths 8 to 10.

qa.q: How did Francis feel after missing the planned study?
qa.a: Francis felt guilty and tense, crossing out the day so hard the pen went through.

qa.q: What could Francis do instead of the no-breaks Sunday?
qa.a: Spread the missed chemistry over a couple of spare slots in the week and keep cricket, treating the wedding as a normal interruption rather than a failure.

qa.q: How might Lokesh have seen Francis at the wedding?
qa.a: Lokesh probably saw a friend too tense to enjoy one evening, and kept trying to help Francis relax.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose disciplined, colour-coded timetable turns into guilt and self-punishment when a family event interrupts it.

passage: On the wall above Kishore's cot in Motihari hung a timetable in four colours: blue for maths, green for biology, red for revision, yellow for rest. There was not much yellow. On Saturday his father's back gave out and someone had to mind the grain shop. Kishore sat behind the scales all day, weighing rice, his biology notes open under the counter. He read the same page nine times. That night he lit the lamp and began squeezing the whole lost day into the night, determined to pay back every hour. Pankaj, passing, saw the light at one in the morning and tapped on the window. 'Still?' 'I wasted today.' 'You ran the shop so your father could rest. That's wasted?' Kishore looked at the colours. For the first time the chart looked less like a plan than a bill he owed.

qa.q: Which colour on Kishore's timetable stood for rest?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: What was Kishore feeling when he began paying back the lost hours at night?
qa.a: He felt guilty and driven, as if helping at the shop were a debt he had to punish himself for.

qa.q: What could Kishore change in his timetable after this?
qa.a: Add more yellow and a few spare slots for days like this, so an interruption means moving work, not staying up half the night.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Kishore's Saturday?
qa.a: Pankaj sees a day well spent helping his father, not wasted, and is worried to find him still up at one.

grounding: Shows a teenager whose disciplined timetable becomes self-punishment when a family need interrupts it.

passage: The drilling next door started at eight on Wednesday and didn't stop. Vasudha tried earplugs, then the balcony, then the stairwell. By six she had done one of her three planned maths chapters. Last year she would have stayed up till two to finish. Instead she opened her planner, wrote 'noise day, 1 of 3' beside Wednesday, and moved the other two chapters into Sunday's empty buffer box, which was there for exactly this. Underneath she added: 'Drilling all week. Library tomorrow?' Preeti messaged at ten: 'Night study at mine? We'll finish everything tonight!' Vasudha smiled at the phone. 'Sleep is on my timetable too. Library at nine?' She switched off the lamp at half past ten.

qa.q: How many of her three maths chapters did Vasudha finish on Wednesday?
qa.a: One.

qa.q: What does Vasudha smiling at Preeti's message suggest she felt?
qa.a: She felt calm and steady, touched by the offer but secure enough in her plan to choose sleep.

qa.q: Which part of Vasudha's plan helped most on a bad day, and why?
qa.a: The empty buffer box on Sunday; it let her move the missed chapters without panic or an all-nighter.

qa.q: How might Preeti feel about Vasudha's reply?
qa.a: Preeti might be a little disappointed, but the library offer keeps them studying together without losing sleep.

grounding: Shows a teenager who builds slack into a study plan, treats a noisy, lost day as information rather than failure, and keeps sleep in the plan.

passage: Aditi's streak chart on the fridge in their Hyderabad flat had three empty boxes in a row: Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday. Her younger brother pointed. 'You broke it!' The old Aditi would have torn the chart down. Instead she sat at the dining table and studied the gaps. All three were rehearsal days for the school's Kuchipudi show, when she got home at eight with aching feet. 'So it's not that I'm lazy,' she told Salma on the phone. 'Forty-five minutes on rehearsal days was never real.' She redrew the chart: forty-five minutes on free days, fifteen on rehearsal days, and a line at the bottom in red: lights out 10.30. 'Fifteen minutes counts?' Salma asked. 'Fifteen every day beats forty-five sometimes,' Aditi said.

qa.q: Which days were the empty boxes on Aditi's chart?
qa.a: Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel looking at the gaps, compared with the old Aditi?
qa.a: She felt calm and curious rather than guilty, studying the gaps for a pattern instead of tearing the chart down.

qa.q: What did Aditi learn from the missed days, and how did she use it?
qa.a: They were all rehearsal days, so she set a realistic fifteen minutes for those days and kept a fixed lights-out time.

qa.q: Why might Salma ask whether fifteen minutes counts?
qa.a: Salma may think study only matters in long blocks, and be surprised that Aditi values doing a little every day.

grounding: Shows a teenager who treats missed study days as information, builds a realistic plan with a fixed bedtime, and values consistency over perfection.

passage:
'Lokesh, lights off at ten? Your test is tomorrow.'
'That's the plan, Papa. Sleep is in it.'
'In my day we studied till the milkman came.'
'And did it work?'
Ramesh laughed. 'Sometimes.'
'I wrote down every day I missed this month. Look. Monday I planned five hours after tuition. I did one. Wednesday, same.'
'So you were lazy on Mondays and Wednesdays?'
'No. Tuition finishes at seven on those days. Five hours was never possible. Now I plan one hour on those days and more on Saturday. Every day since, I've done what the plan says.'
Ramesh looked at his son's notebook, columns of small ticks. 'Every day?'
'Not perfectly. But every day.'
'Hm.' Ramesh switched off the light himself. 'Goodnight, planner sahib.'

qa.q: What time does tuition finish on Mondays and Wednesdays?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's calm reply to 'lazy' show about how he feels about the missed days?
qa.a: He feels settled, not guilty; he treats the missed days as information about his tuition schedule, not proof of laziness.

qa.q: Why is Lokesh's change to one hour on tuition days sensible?
qa.a: It fits the plan to real life so he can keep it every day; consistency counts for more than an impossible five hours.

qa.q: How might Ramesh feel as he switches off the light himself?
qa.a: Ramesh seems amused and a little impressed, even proud, won over by his son's plan.

grounding: Shows a teenager who keeps a realistic plan with sleep built in, reads missed days as information, and values consistency over perfection.

passage:
Monday. Hafsa wanted to split the street-play project into roles and dates. 'Let's see how it flows,' Nitin said. 'We'll know what's needed when it's needed.'
Thursday. An hour before the show, the college moved it from the open lawn to a narrow corridor. Everyone panicked except Nitin. He re-blocked every scene in forty minutes, turned the corridor into a railway platform, and the crowd loved it.
The next Monday. The written report was due at five. At four, Hafsa asked for Nitin's section. He hadn't started. 'You said we'd know what's needed,' she said, voice tight. 'This was needed.' Nitin's ears burned. He wrote until six, apologised to the professor for the delay, and that night set three dates in his phone with alarms: rehearsal, report, show. 'Everything else,' he told Hafsa, 'I'll still wing.'

qa.q: Where did the college move the show on Thursday?
qa.a: From the open lawn to a narrow corridor.

qa.q: What did Nitin feel when Hafsa said 'This was needed'?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and guilty, his ears burning, seeing that his 'see how it flows' had left her waiting.

qa.q: What anchors did Nitin set, and why do they suit his style?
qa.a: Three dates with alarms for rehearsal, report and show; they fix the shared commitments while leaving him free to adapt everything else.

qa.q: How did Hafsa experience Nitin's style across those two weeks?
qa.a: She saw it rescue the show on Thursday, then felt let down and tense when the report deadline came without his part.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose flexible, decide-late style shines when plans change but fails a shared deadline until he sets deliberate anchors.

passage: Kishore, you ask why I write only three kinds of things in ink on my calendar. At your age I never booked anything. Trains, jobs, plans, I decided on the platform. And I was good at it: when a shoot in Hampi was cancelled, I found a village fair in two hours and came back with better photos than anyone. Editors loved me for it. Then my friend Latha asked me to photograph her wedding. I said yes, of course, and wrote it nowhere. That week a magazine offered me Ladakh. I went. I remembered on the plane. Latha didn't speak to me for two years. After that I kept my freedom for everything except three things: deadlines, promises, people. Those go in ink. Everything else, your Sarita Bua still decides on the platform.

qa.q: What did Sarita do when the Hampi shoot was cancelled?
qa.a: She found a village fair in two hours and came back with better photos than anyone.

qa.q: What might Sarita have felt when she remembered the wedding on the plane?
qa.a: She probably felt a sinking guilt and shame, realising she had broken a promise to a friend.

qa.q: What choice in the story changed how Sarita worked afterwards?
qa.a: Deciding to put deadlines, promises and people in ink, while staying spontaneous about everything else.

qa.q: How was Latha affected by Sarita's choice to go to Ladakh?
qa.a: Latha lost her photographer on her wedding day, felt let down, and didn't speak to Sarita for two years.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a young adult whose spontaneous style works well with change but breaks a shared commitment, until she sets fixed anchors.

passage: The rain came down at noon on fest day, and the open lawn turned to mud. Sabina didn't blink. Within twenty minutes she had dragged their stall under the library stairwell, chalked RAIN SPECIAL: GINGER CHAI on a board, and sent Asif to call it through the corridors. By two there was a queue. 'You're a genius,' Asif said. At four the burner sputtered and died. The gas. On Friday Asif had asked her to book the refill, and she had said, 'I'll see how the day goes.' Now thirty people stood waiting with cups. Asif just looked at her. Sabina's cheeks went hot. That night, on the back of the chai board, she wrote three things that would never again be 'I'll see': gas, cash box, closing time. Everything else could stay open.

qa.q: What did Sabina chalk on the board?
qa.a: RAIN SPECIAL: GINGER CHAI.

qa.q: What does Sabina's cheeks going hot suggest?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and guilty, knowing her 'I'll see' about the gas had let Asif and the customers down.

qa.q: What is the point of the three things Sabina wrote down?
qa.a: They are anchors for shared commitments, so her flexibility stays for everything else while the essentials don't slip.

qa.q: What might Asif have felt when he just looked at her?
qa.a: Asif was probably frustrated and let down, having asked about the gas on Friday, even after praising her quick thinking.

grounding: Shows a young adult whose spontaneous style rescues a stall in the rain but lets a shared commitment slip, prompting fixed anchors.

subtype: Living with a very careful partner or roommate [Receiver]
passage: In the Pune flat she shared with Gargi, Devika never worried about bills. Gargi's chart on the fridge said who paid the electricity, whose week it was for the bathroom, when the gas cylinder was due. It felt safe. It also felt like living inside an exam. Gargi re-folded Devika's towels. She moved Devika's spice jars into alphabetical order. On Tuesday Devika came home to a sticky note on her own shelf: 'Please keep this area tidy.' She stood in the kitchen, jaw tight, and finally admitted to herself that she was angry. That night she knocked on Gargi's door. 'The fridge chart, please never stop. That's a real help. But my shelf and my towels, that's just how you like things. Can those be mine?' Gargi flushed. 'I didn't know it bothered you.' 'I never said. I should have.'

qa.q: What did the sticky note on Devika's shelf say?
qa.a: 'Please keep this area tidy.'

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as she stood in the kitchen with her jaw tight?
qa.a: She felt angry and watched, a resentment that had built quietly behind the relief of never worrying about bills.

qa.q: Why did Devika's way of raising it work?
qa.a: She thanked Gargi for the chart and plainly named the shelf and towels as preferences, so it didn't feel like an attack.

qa.q: How might Gargi feel on hearing this?
qa.a: Gargi was embarrassed and surprised, flushing, since she hadn't known her tidying bothered Devika.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels both safe and corrected living with a very orderly flatmate, and says plainly what is a preference and what is a real need.

subtype: Living with a very careful partner or roommate [Receiver]
passage:
'You left the milk lid loose again.'
'Asif, it's been in the fridge ten minutes.'
'It spills if someone moves it.'
Sudha put her cup down. 'Can I say something without it becoming a fight?'
'Okay.'
'I love that you pay the electricity bill the day it comes. Since we married I've never once worried about the gas running out. That's real, and I'm grateful.'
'But?'
'But every day there's a lid, or a towel, or how I stack plates. I feel like I'm being marked.'
Asif was quiet. 'I don't mean it like that.'
'I know. So tell me which ones are real needs for you, and which are just how you like it.'
He thought. 'The gas knob. The door lock. Those scare me. The lid is a preference.'
'Then I'll do the scary ones every time. The lid I'll try, but no reminders.'
'Deal.'

qa.q: Which two things did Asif call real needs?
qa.a: The gas knob and the door lock.

qa.q: How does Sudha feel about the daily corrections?
qa.a: She feels watched and marked, and a quiet resentment has been building, even though she is grateful for his carefulness.

qa.q: Why did asking 'which are needs and which are preferences' help?
qa.a: It separated what truly matters to Asif from habits, so Sudha could commit to the essentials and they could drop the rest.

qa.q: What did Asif learn about how his reminders felt?
qa.a: He learned that what he saw as small corrections made Sudha feel marked, which he never meant.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels both secure and corrected living with a very careful partner, and plainly separates his real needs from preferences.

subtype: Living with a very careful partner or roommate [Receiver]
passage: When I moved to Delhi for college, I shared a one-room flat in Laxmi Nagar with my older brother Tushar. I'm Sunaina, and I'll admit it: with Tushar around, I never once worried about rent day or the water bill. He kept a notebook for it, dated and ruled. But he also had opinions about how I folded my dupatta, where my shoes went, why my books were on the bed. For months I said nothing and just seethed. Then one night I threw my shoes at the rack and said something awful. We didn't speak for two days. What finally worked was boring. I made two lists and showed him. Keep doing: the rent notebook. Just your preference: my dupatta. He read it twice and laughed. 'Fine. Your dupatta, your problem.'

qa.q: Where did Sunaina and Tushar share a flat?
qa.a: In a one-room flat in Laxmi Nagar, Delhi.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling during the months of saying nothing?
qa.a: Sunaina felt resentful, silently seething at the constant comments, until it burst out over the shoes.

qa.q: Why did the two lists work better than the outburst?
qa.a: They named plainly what was a real need, the rent notebook, and what was only preference, without attacking Tushar.

qa.q: How might Tushar have felt reading the lists?
qa.a: He seemed relieved and amused, laughing, perhaps glad that his careful notebook was valued.

grounding: Shows a young adult who feels safe about bills but corrected by a very orderly sibling flatmate, and learns to say plainly what is a need and what is a preference.

passage: At the milk cooperative on the edge of Anand, everyone knew: if the chilling-tank log was missing, Bhavna had it. If a farmer's payment slip was wrong, Bhavna had already caught it. Lalit, who sat across from her, had watched her stay back three evenings in a row that month, fixing entries others had left half done. Nobody said thank you; they just said, 'Bhavna will see.' On Monday she didn't come in. Her mother phoned: fever and exhaustion, and the doctor had told her to rest. By Tuesday the tank log was a mess and two farmers were arguing at the counter. Lalit sorted the slips as best he could and felt a small, sick shame. He had been one of the ones saying 'Bhavna will see.' That evening he began a list of everything she did, to divide among the team.

qa.q: What did people say whenever something was missing?
qa.a: 'Bhavna will see.'

qa.q: What did Lalit feel while sorting the slips on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt a small, sick shame, knowing he too had leaned on Bhavna without ever thanking her.

qa.q: What could the team do so Bhavna isn't overloaded when she returns?
qa.a: Share out her tasks, as Lalit's list begins to, thank her openly, and stop leaving half-done work for her to fix.

qa.q: What might those evenings of fixing others' entries have been like for Bhavna?
qa.a: She was probably tired and unappreciated, quietly carrying extra work until she was exhausted.

grounding: Shows a colleague noticing that the most reliable person on the team has been over-relied on and unthanked until she burns out.

passage: In her first month at the small design studio in Lisbon, Freya noticed that every question ended the same way: 'Ask Sofia.' Sofia knew which client hated green, which printer jammed, where last year's logo files lived. When a brochure went out with a wrong phone number, it was Sofia who stayed late reprinting it, and on Friday the manager thanked 'the whole team'. Freya saw Sofia's jaw tighten. The next Wednesday, leaving at nine, Freya passed Sofia's desk. The lamp was still on; Sofia sat pressing her palms into her eyes. Freya hesitated, then pulled up a chair. 'Show me the printer orders,' she said. 'I'll do them from now on.' Sofia looked up, surprised, and for a moment didn't seem able to speak.

qa.q: What did the manager say on Friday?
qa.a: The manager thanked 'the whole team'.

qa.q: What was Freya feeling when she hesitated at Sofia's desk?
qa.a: Freya felt uncomfortable and concerned, unsure whether to intrude but worried by how worn out Sofia looked.

qa.q: What could the manager do differently?
qa.a: Name Sofia's work when thanking people and spread her tasks around, so the most reliable person isn't quietly overloaded.

qa.q: Why might Sofia struggle to speak when Freya offered help?
qa.a: Sofia is probably exhausted and so used to going unthanked that a simple offer of help moved and surprised her.

grounding: Shows a new colleague noticing that the person everyone relies on is unthanked and overloaded, and stepping in to share the load.

passage: On Ward 6 the night staff had a joke: the handover sheet was either 'Seema's' or 'a mess'. Gurleen had worked beside Seema for a year and never seen her forget a thing: which patient hated the cold, whose family called at ten, which drip needed changing before the doctors' round. So when a shift fell empty, Sister Mathew always asked Seema first, and Seema always said yes. This month Gurleen counted four extra shifts. Last night Seema snapped at a trainee over a missing signature, then apologised in the pantry, eyes wet. Gurleen felt her own stomach knot. In the morning she knocked on Sister Mathew's door. 'We all lean on Seema, and nobody says thanks. She's running on empty. Can we stop asking her first?' Sister Mathew put her pen down and opened the roster.

qa.q: How many extra shifts did Seema do this month?
qa.a: Four.

qa.q: What did Gurleen feel after seeing Seema in the pantry?
qa.a: Gurleen felt worried, her stomach knotting at how exhausted Seema had become.

qa.q: Was Gurleen right to go to Sister Mathew? Why?
qa.a: Yes; the problem lay in how shifts were handed out, so the person managing the roster needed to know and change it.

qa.q: What might the extra shifts have been like for Seema?
qa.a: Seema likely felt trusted but worn down, unable to refuse, and so tired that she snapped and then cried.

grounding: Shows a colleague who notices that a reliable nurse is over-relied on and unthanked to the point of burnout, and raises it with the person in charge.

passage: On the local bus to Thrissur, Aditi waved at the conductor, a man with a goat, and three schoolgirls. Each time someone waved back, she squealed louder. When she reached for a stranger's jasmine garland, her mother Gopika caught her hand. 'Wave, yes. Pull, no.' Aditi waved at the garland instead, beaming. At home, alone in the courtyard, she sat quietly sucking her thumb, until the neighbours' children came over and she ran to them, squealing.

qa.q: Who did Aditi wave at on the bus?
qa.a: The conductor, a man with a goat, and three schoolgirls.

qa.q: What does Aditi squealing louder each time someone waves back suggest?
qa.a: She feels excited and delighted, her energy rising with every person who responds.

qa.q: How did Gopika teach a gentle limit?
qa.a: She caught Aditi's hand and said 'Wave, yes. Pull, no,' keeping the friendliness but stopping the grab.

qa.q: How might the stranger with the garland feel?
qa.a: Probably amused rather than annoyed, especially once Gopika stopped the grab and Aditi simply waved.

grounding: Shows a toddler who waves at strangers and grows louder and livelier around people, quieter alone, while a parent teaches a gentle limit.

passage: At the park near their flat in Lagos, Chidi ran straight to the sandpit where two older girls were digging, sat down beside them and shouted, 'Me dig!' When one girl laughed, he laughed louder and flung sand in the air. Then he tried to hug the smaller girl, who shrank back. His father Daniel knelt. 'She's shy. High five, not hug.' Chidi slapped her palm gently. On the walk home, alone in his pushchair, he went quiet and heavy-eyed.

qa.q: What did Chidi shout at the sandpit?
qa.a: 'Me dig!'

qa.q: Why did Chidi laugh louder and fling sand?
qa.a: Being with the other children made him excited and full of energy.

qa.q: Why was 'High five, not hug' a good limit?
qa.a: It kept Chidi friendly while respecting the shy girl, giving him another way to connect.

qa.q: How might the smaller girl feel when Chidi tries to hug her?
qa.a: She probably felt startled and uncomfortable, shrinking back from a stranger's hug.

grounding: Shows a toddler seeking other children to play beside, getting loud with excitement and quiet when alone, while a parent teaches a gentle limit.

passage:
Monday. Rain all day, just Deepika and Papa in the flat. She dragged her doll about, whining, and fell asleep early.
Wednesday. At the building's Ganpati pandal, Deepika waved at every aunty, danced to the dhol and shrieked with joy. In her excitement she grabbed a boy's hair. Santosh knelt. 'Soft hands.' She stroked it instead.
Friday. At the park she marched up to a new toddler, patted his arm gently and said, 'Friend!'

qa.q: What did Deepika do at the Ganpati pandal?
qa.a: She waved at every aunty, danced to the dhol and shrieked with joy.

qa.q: Why was Deepika whining on Monday?
qa.a: Stuck indoors with only Papa, she seemed bored and low, missing the people who lift her energy.

qa.q: How did Santosh's 'Soft hands' help by Friday?
qa.a: It taught a gentle limit without stopping her friendliness, and by Friday she patted a new toddler gently.

qa.q: How might the boy at the pandal feel when Deepika grabs his hair?
qa.a: He probably felt startled and hurt, even though Deepika was only excited.

grounding: Shows a toddler whose energy dips alone and rises in a crowd, and who learns a gentle limit from a parent.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage: At the parent-teacher meeting, Ramesh sat on a tiny chair between his two children. Kamal, six, had already told Ms. Pinto about the lizard in the bathroom and his new shoes. Chhavi, five, held Ramesh's sleeve and said nothing. 'Chhavi is bright,' said Ms. Pinto, 'but she must speak up like her brother.' Ramesh felt the familiar pull. At home Kamal chattered till bedtime; Chhavi needed quiet mornings with her drawings. 'She talks,' he said. 'Just not in a crowd. Yesterday she told me a whole story, alone with me. I don't want her made into Kamal.' Chhavi's grip loosened.

qa.q: What did Kamal tell Ms. Pinto about?
qa.a: The lizard in the bathroom and his new shoes.

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when Ms. Pinto compared the children?
qa.a: He felt the familiar pull between them, uneasy and protective, not wanting Chhavi pushed to be like Kamal.

qa.q: What did Ramesh's reply get right?
qa.a: It explained that Chhavi talks in her own way, alone and quietly, and refused to force her to match her brother.

qa.q: How might Chhavi feel when her grip loosens?
qa.a: Chhavi probably feels relieved and safe, understood by Ramesh instead of pushed.

grounding: Shows a parent pulled between a chatty child and a quiet one, who refuses to force them into sameness.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage:
Monday. At a loud birthday party Uma pushed both children onto the dance floor. Nakul whooped; Pooja, five, hid behind the curtain and cried.
Wednesday. Worn out by Nakul's chatter, Uma declared quiet time for both. Nakul, four, kicked the sofa and wailed. Pooja finally smiled.
Saturday. Uma sent Nakul to the park with the neighbour's boys and sat alone with Pooja, rolling dough in silence. When Nakul burst back full of stories, she listened to every one. That night she felt tired, but less torn.

qa.q: Where did Pooja hide at the party?
qa.a: Behind the curtain.

qa.q: How did Uma feel on Saturday night, and why?
qa.a: She felt tired but less torn, because each child had got the kind of attention they needed.

qa.q: What did Uma learn from Monday and Wednesday?
qa.a: Forcing both children into the same thing upset one of them each time; giving each a different kind of time worked better.

qa.q: What was Wednesday's quiet time like for Nakul?
qa.a: Nakul felt frustrated and trapped, kicking the sofa and wailing, because quiet suits Pooja, not him.

grounding: Shows a parent of a lively child and a quiet child learning that forcing the same activity hurts both, and that each needs different attention.

subtype: Parent of an extravert and an introvert [Receiver]
passage: The power went out at seven, and the whole flat shrank to one candlelit room. Suraj, six, talked without stopping: shadows, lizards, what if the lights never came back. Mira, four, pressed her hands over her ears and began to whimper. Urmila felt pulled in two. 'Suraj, shush!' she snapped, and his face crumpled. She took a breath. Then she gave Mira the torch and the quiet corner with her picture book, and took Suraj to the doorway to make shadow animals, whispering. Soon Mira was turning pages, and Suraj was giggling at a shadow crocodile.

qa.q: What did Urmila give Mira?
qa.a: The torch and the quiet corner with her picture book.

qa.q: How did Urmila feel when both children needed her at once?
qa.a: She felt pulled in two and snapped, then stopped to calm herself.

qa.q: What worked better than 'Suraj, shush'?
qa.a: Giving each child a different kind of attention: quiet space for Mira and whispered shadow play with Suraj.

qa.q: What was it like for Suraj when Urmila snapped?
qa.a: Suraj felt hurt and his face crumpled; his chatter was how he coped with the dark.

grounding: Shows a parent pulled between a chatty child and a quiet one during a power cut, who finds a different kind of attention for each.

passage:
Monday. By lunch on her first day at the new school, Vandana knew eleven names and was captain of the kho-kho game.
Wednesday. Silent reading. Vandana's pencil tapped, her feet swung, and she whispered jokes to the girl beside her until Mrs. Fernandes moved her desk to the front.
Saturday. Vandana's birthday: fifteen friends, music, a treasure hunt she had planned herself. Twenty minutes in, Imran's mother came to fetch him. Vandana's smile slipped. 'He didn't like it?' Later her father said, 'Did you see him by the speaker with his hands over his ears? He told you twice it was loud.' She hadn't heard. On Sunday she phoned Imran. 'Want to come over? Just us. Carrom. No music.' 'Okay,' he said, and she could hear him smiling.

qa.q: How many names did Vandana know by lunch on her first day?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Vandana feel when Imran left the party early?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused, her smile slipping as she wondered whether he didn't like it.

qa.q: What did Vandana's Sunday phone call get right?
qa.a: It offered Imran the kind of time he enjoys, just the two of them and no music, once she realised she had missed his cues.

qa.q: What was the party like for Imran?
qa.a: It was too loud for him; he stood by the speaker covering his ears and had said so twice, so he left early.

grounding: Shows a child who makes friends quickly, leads games and fidgets in silent work, but misses a quieter friend's cues until a parent points them out.

passage: Darshan, you talk just like I did. At your age in Ludhiana, I knew every child on our street by the second day. I picked the cricket teams and chattered through the quiet reading hour until Master ji said, 'Amandeep, one more word and you sit beside me.' But my best friend Jaspal was different. One summer he stopped coming to matches, and I kept shouting at his window, 'Come! We need you!' I thought he was sulking. Then one evening I saw him on his roof, holding his kite, not flying it. I climbed up and, for once, said nothing. Then he told me his mother was in hospital. I sat with him every evening after that. Your Nanu learned to be quiet on that roof.

qa.q: Where did Amandeep find Jaspal one evening?
qa.a: On his roof, holding his kite, not flying it.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel about Jaspal staying away from the matches at first?
qa.a: Amandeep felt impatient and a bit annoyed, thinking Jaspal was sulking, and kept shouting at his window.

qa.q: What choice on the roof changed things between the two friends?
qa.a: Amandeep climbed up and, for once, said nothing; that quiet gave Jaspal the space to share that his mother was in hospital.

qa.q: What might that summer have been like for Jaspal?
qa.a: Jaspal was worried and sad about his mother and needed quiet, so the shouts to come and play were probably hard to answer.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a talkative child who leads games and struggles in quiet hours, missing a friend's need for space until he notices it.

passage: It had rained since morning, so recess was indoors, and Ritu could hardly bear it. Forty minutes of silent seat work had left her knees jiggling under the desk. The moment the bell rang she jumped up. 'Dumb charades! Girls versus boys!' In two minutes she had teams, a scorer and a chalk list of films. Only Pallavi stayed at her desk, a library book open, not turning pages. 'Pallavi, you're on my team!' Ritu tugged her arm. 'I said I don't want to.' 'Come on, it's fun!' 'Ritu, stop.' Pallavi's voice cracked. Ritu let go. Now she saw it: the red eyes, the unturned page. Pallavi had said no twice already that morning. Ritu picked someone else for her team and sat down beside Pallavi, saying nothing.

qa.q: What game did Ritu organise?
qa.a: Dumb charades, girls versus boys.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling during the forty minutes of silent seat work?
qa.a: Ritu felt restless and bored, knees jiggling, longing for company and noise.

qa.q: What could Ritu have noticed earlier?
qa.a: That Pallavi had already said no twice and was staring at an unturned page; a quiet 'Are you okay?' before tugging her arm would have helped.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when Ritu tugged her arm?
qa.a: Pallavi felt upset and overwhelmed, her voice cracking, on a morning that was already hard.

grounding: Shows a child who gains energy from company and leads games but, restless after silent work, misses a friend's quiet cues until they become obvious.

passage: On the first morning of summer camp at the community centre, the other children rushed to the craft tables. Dilnaz stood by the water cooler for twenty minutes, watching: who shared the glue, who grabbed, who laughed kindly. Aunty Rosy, the camp leader, came over, frowning. 'Aren't you happy here?' 'I am,' Dilnaz said. 'I'm just looking first.' Then she walked to the end of the table where one boy, Darshan, was carefully cutting paper birds, and sat beside him. By Friday they were a pair, finishing each other's kites, and she still spent snack break reading alone on the steps, humming.

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz stand on the first morning?
qa.a: By the water cooler.

qa.q: Why did Dilnaz watch for twenty minutes before joining?
qa.a: She felt calmer seeing the group first and noticing who was kind; she wasn't unhappy, just careful.

qa.q: How could Aunty Rosy support a child like Dilnaz?
qa.a: Trust her 'I'm just looking first', give her time, and not treat reading alone at snack break as a problem.

qa.q: How might Darshan see Dilnaz sitting down beside him?
qa.a: Darshan probably felt glad to have one steady friend who shared his careful way of working.

grounding: Shows a child who watches a new group before joining, prefers one close friend, and enjoys time alone without being unhappy.

passage:
Saturday night. At his cousin's sangeet, Ojas danced, laughed with the cousins and ate three helpings of jalebi. By eleven his ears rang and his smile felt stuck on.
Sunday. He stayed in his room all morning with a comic and the door half shut. 'Are you sad, Ojas?' Mummy asked, peering in. 'No. Just empty. Not a bad empty. I need quiet.' She left a glass of lassi and closed the door.
Monday. After school he cycled to Amandeep's, his one best friend. They built a ramp for two hours, barely talking, and Ojas came home humming.

qa.q: What did Ojas eat three helpings of at the sangeet?
qa.a: Jalebi.

qa.q: How was Ojas feeling on Sunday morning, in his own words?
qa.a: He felt drained, 'empty' but not sad; he needed quiet to recover after the busy party.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Ojas recover?
qa.a: She asked instead of assuming, then left lassi and closed the door, giving him the solitude he needed.

qa.q: What might Amandeep enjoy about Monday's ramp-building with Ojas?
qa.a: Amandeep seems comfortable with long, easy silences, so two hours of building side by side felt good for both.

grounding: Shows a child who enjoys a busy party but is drained afterwards, recovers through solitude, and prefers one close friend.

passage: Jeevan, you ask why I slipped away from the Diwali party last night. Your Sonali Aaji was the same at ten, in our chawl in Pune. At every festival there were fifty people in two rooms, and I loved them all, for about an hour. Then my head would fill up like a pot boiling over, and I would slip away to the stairwell with a book. My mother called it rudeness. 'Why are you so unfriendly? People will talk.' I wasn't unhappy. I was full. One Diwali my Mavshi found me on the stairs and read beside me without a word. After a while I went back in, laughing again. She told my mother, 'Let her have the stairs. She comes back better.' From then on, the stairs were mine.

qa.q: Where did Sonali go when her head filled up?
qa.a: To the stairwell with a book.

qa.q: How did Sonali feel when her mother called her unfriendly?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and misunderstood, because she wasn't unhappy, only full.

qa.q: What turning point made the stairs Sonali's?
qa.a: Her Mavshi sat and read with her, saw her come back laughing, and told her mother to let her have the stairs.

qa.q: How might Sonali's mother have felt at those festivals?
qa.a: Her mother seems worried about what people would say, reading Sonali's slipping away as rudeness.

grounding: Shows, in an elder's memory, a child who enjoys people but is drained by busy gatherings and recovers through solitude, not unhappiness.
